newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian press ponders who killed unionist leader.
newsitem.headline: Algerian press ponders who killed unionist leader.

text.p: Algerian trade union boss Abdelhak Benhamouda, gunned down in central Algiers, gasped out as he died: "Kamel, my brother, they have betrayed us", an Algerian newspaper said on Wednesday.

His words, the ambush in May 1st Square on Tuesday, and the escape in the heavily policed city of the gunmen -- said by the government to be Moslem fundamentalists -- raised widespread questions on Wednesday over the killing and its motives.

Algeria's independent newspapers all asked: "Who killed Benhamouda?", one of Algerian President Liamine Zeroual's main political backers and a powerful figure who was preparing to step down from his union and start his own political party.
El Khabar quoted Benhamouda's last words as he fell into the arms of a brother unionist in the million-strong UGTA (Union Generale des Travailleurs Algeriens) he headed.
It added: "No fewer than 14 bullets had been emptied into him", and said his death was "classed among all the political assassinations through which the country has lived".

El Khabar cited among them the killing in Annaba town of President Mohamed Boudiaf in June 1992, for which Lembarek Boumaraafi, a member of his own security force was convicted, sentenced to death, but remains in prison.

As ripples from the killing spread in the North African country and abroad, analysts in France who closely follow events in its former colony, said Benhamouda appeared to have been killed by a rival faction within the ruling hierarchy.
One pointed out that Zeroual described him as having been shot by "traitors" rather than "terrorists", which is Algiers' usual official term for fundamentalists.

The Algerian newspaper El Watan commented: "...from the announcement of the creation of his party, Benhamouda has appeared...as a key man in the political debate. And at the centre of intense political controversy.
"Who assassinated Benhamouda. Who profited from this crime. A question all the world is asking. Is it the FIDA (Front Islamique du Djihad en Algerie)...Or is it a political paying of scores?"
Several Algerian newspapers, including the government-run El Moudjahid, said Benhamouda died with his gun in his hand.
L'Authentique said: "He fired back before succumbing."

Another independent paper Liberte asked whether Benhamouda had died because he was "the new political man who was preparing...to upset the national chessboard...Who killed him, or rather, who ordered his elimination?"
Even the official newspaper El Moudjahid said: "It is not easy to understand this killing and the reasons which truly motivated it."
The UGTA leader had escaped one earlier assassination bid and his brother was killed in another, blamed on Moslem rebels.
Benhamouda, a vociferous anti-Islamist, was the best known figure to die in over two weeks of intensified bloodshed which has marked the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
Zeroual, who only four days earlier had vowed to eradicate "terrorism" from Algeria, mourned Benhamouda's death as a loss for the country and its workers.

Benhamouda will be buried in Algiers on Thursday, a union source said. "His body will be displayed in the Maison du Peuple (House of the People - union headquarters) before the burial in al-Alia cemetery," the source said.
The cemetery is reserved for senior Algerian leaders, those who died in leading Algeria's 1954-1962 war of independece against France, and those who have died as martyrs since.

Among those interred there is President Mohamed Boudiaf, gunned down in the eastern town of Annaba June 1992 after six months in power, and former military intelligence chief and prime minister Kasdi Merbah. He was killed in 1993 near Algiers in an ambush blamed by the authorities on Moslem rebels.

About 60,000 people have died in the five-year-old conflict, which erupted in 1992 after the authorities cancelled a general election dominated by Islamists. New elections are promised before July this year.
